summary:
Yucatán operates an administrative route to legal gender recognition. A 2024 reform to the state's Civil Registry Law, published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024, created a procedure through which transgender people can update the legal gender recorded on their identity documents without obtaining a court order. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of 11 March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis. This is the fact a trans visitor's document situation turns on when entering or being stopped in the state: the gender marker on a Mexican identity document issued here can be corrected through an administrative filing rather than litigation.

Yucatán stands under Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition, which remains unfinished and uneven across the country; the administrative procedure described above is the layer specific to this state.

Relationship recognition for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship arrived first through the courts and then through statute. The Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled on 1 July 2013 that two petitioners were able to marry, and the first same-sex couple legally married in the state on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015, and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán then passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended the secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022, so marriage in the state now rests on statute as well as court order.

Yucatán is listed as enacting a ban on conversion therapy on 25 August 2021, placing a protective statute on the books alongside the state-level bans elsewhere in Mexico.
tangentialFactors:
Yucatán's recognition procedure is not exceptional but neither is it universal. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and named six states whose legislatures had enacted none. Yucatán sits within the group of states that has acted; the six named states have not.

The conversion-therapy ban Yucatán enacted on 25 August 2021 belongs to a wider state-level pattern rather than standing alone, running alongside the ban adopted by Mexico City on 31 July 2020 and those of other states.

Social context differs from the statutory text. Sexual diversity is documented as tolerated among Yucatán Maya groups, which bears on how a gender-nonconforming visitor is likely to be received in the state's interior and Maya communities as distinct from its formal legal position.
localsOnly:
For residents, the 2024 Civil Registry Law reform means the legal gender on a state-issued identity document can be corrected through an administrative procedure at the registry, without a court order. The reform was published in the Diario Oficial of 26 April 2024 on yucatan.gob.mx.

Residents' relationship rights rest on a settled statutory footing: the Congress of Yucatán's constitutional amendment of 7 September 2021 and the secondary-legislation amendment of 1 March 2022 followed the litigation of 2013 to 2015, so a couple no longer needs a court ruling to marry in the state.

The conversion-therapy ban enacted on 25 August 2021 is a resident-facing protection, restricting the practice within the state's territory.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Yucatán-specific figures are sourced here on processing times, fees, documentation requirements or refusal rates for the administrative recognition procedure, so the practical ease of using it is unresolved.

No Yucatán-specific incidents of violence against trans people, and no state-level homicide or complaint statistics for Yucatán, appear in the inventory; the national pattern of killings and impunity described in the parent record cannot be assumed to distribute evenly across states.

Whether the 25 August 2021 conversion-therapy ban has been enforced, and whether any complaints have been brought under it, is not sourced.

The scope of the recognition procedure, including whether it addresses birth-certificate surgery requirements or non-binary markers, is not sourced.
